item.title: Why Am I So Angry All the Time? Practical Tips to Overcome Anger
item.description:
The Heart Angle

It is important to discuss anger from a heartfelt perspective, although anger is not known for being a heartfelt emotion. When a person asks why they are so angry all the time, the root cause may not be known, so the question will only be partially answered.

The root cause for a great deal of the anger that is experienced derives from issues or matters of the heart. There is a saying that says there is a thin line between love and hate. Indeed, it is so thin that at times their distance from one another is small.

As a therapist, I have found that when anger is unpacked, it often stems from heartbreak caused by disappointment, loss, grief, lack of progress, feelings of failure, rejection, abandonment, and even a lack of felt love. Anger is often telling you what you are avoiding.

Emotions are the byproduct of the deeper symptoms. What is going on in your heart that is portraying itself as anger? To answer this question, we must go underneath. Your anger is trying to tell you something. The question is: what? This is often what is occurring.

  • There is hurt without clarity.
  • Undealt-with rejection.
  • Unhealed abandonment.
  • You may be feeling powerless.
  • You may be feeling ignored.
  • You may have tolerated something for too long.
  • You may be feeling stuck.
  • You may even be angry because there is a truth somewhere in your life that you have been unwilling or unable to confront.

Take the time to consider each thought. Allow it to sit with you.

Anger and Our Relationship with the Truth

I believe a great deal of anger can be connected to our relationship with truth. Sometimes we are angry because we cannot tell the truth. Sometimes we are angry because we do not want to face the truth. Sometimes we are angry because we are not living according to what we know is true.

Then there are times when we are angry because someone else told us the truth and we were not ready to hear it. The truth can be uncomfortable. Truth can seem threatening. Truth can even seem insulting without the intention of being so.

Maybe you continue saying yes to people when you really want to push back. Yet the deeper problem may not be that people keep asking. The deeper problem may be that you have not been honest about what you can handle. You have trouble admitting your limitations, and you would rather die than have anyone perceive a weakness.

Perhaps you are angry about your lack of professional progression. You are feeling overlooked by your superiors and undervalued. You resent your coworkers for getting what you deserve. You used to love your company and once saw a future there. But now you dread work mornings. Deep down, you know it is time to make a change, but fear has prevented you from making a change.

Truth will also require you to acknowledge when you have participated in your own frustration. There are times when we remain in situations long after we know something must change. Nevertheless, we become angry with people for crossing boundaries we have never verbalized or enforced.

We may even become irritated when others do not recognize needs that we have never expressed. Standing toe to toe with truth means asking yourself what part of the situation belongs to you. That moment may be uncomfortable, but it can help show us where we still have the power to move differently.

Your anger is real. But so is the hurtful and hard-to-face truth underneath it. Jesus said that the truth would make us free. Freedom has never begun with pretending. Freedom requires us to become willing to see what is there. Sometimes anger increases because we are fighting reality that we feel helpless to change.

Think About It, You May Not Be Angry About Today

A major reason why anger can feel disproportionate is that the current situation is carrying the weight of several previous situations. Someone does something tiny, and in return you respond enormously. Ever wonder when you became so upset? The other person may wonder the same thing.

The answer could be that you were not only responding to what happened today, because that is all you can see in the moment. However, you neglected to really comprehend that you were responding to every time you felt overlooked. Not to mention every time you were disappointed, or for each time a promise was broken, or for each conversation that went unresolved.

Think about it, you may not be angry about today, but for every moment you have decided not to say anything. Your anger had been accumulating when experiences that you had in your life were not properly processed. This is why it is not unusual to encounter some people going from zero to one hundred over something that appears insignificant.

The current situation may simply be the final place where everything else came to a head. In those intense moments, ask yourself, “What else am I responding to right now?” The answer could separate today’s frustration from yesterday’s wound.

Practical Tips to Overcome Anger

The goal of overcoming anger is not to become a person who never gets angry. This is unrealistic and not maintainable. The key to overcoming anger is learning how to recognize what your anger is revealing before it begins attempting to take center stage. Your anger becomes more manageable when you have practical steps that can help you move from reacting to your anger toward understanding it and responding differently.

Identify what is happening beneath the anger Instead of “I am upset,” finish the sentence: “I am angry because I felt…” Permit yourself to go above and beyond what may have been your obvious answer. Were you feeling ashamed? Did you feel disregarded? Did you feel powerless? Remember, naming what is at the root of your anger will aid you in understanding what really needs your attention,

Start separating what you can change from what you cannot control Ask: “What am I avoiding?” You may already know what needs to be changed. The hard part may be accepting what that truth may require from us.

Do not shut down speaking what you feel sooner Do not make silence carry something until anger has to announce it. You cannot control another person’s choices. You can control what you participate in. You can decide what you will tolerate. You can also determine what access someone will continue to have to you.

Examine your expectations Determine what was conveyed. Do not make silence carry something until anger has to announce it. Learn to communicate frustration while it is still frustration. Not everything requires confrontation, but important matters should not continually be buried.

Decide what you should be grieving instead of correcting Some things cannot be fixed. They must be mourned. Some things cannot be fixed. They must be mourned. You may be trying to get an apology you will never receive or attempting to change something that has already happened. Grief may be necessary where correction is no longer possible.

Choose what your anger will yield Let it lead to a boundary, conversation, decision, healing work, or change rather than damage. Anger has energy attached to it. Decide where that energy will go. Your anger can destroy something or reveal what needs to be different. The responsibility is deciding what happens next.

item.title: What BPD in Women Looks Like
item.description:
Borderline Personality Disorder is a condition born from complex childhood trauma. A person with BPD experiences crippling loneliness, fear of abandonment, anger control issues, struggles with identity and self-worth, and usually has a history of unstable relationships and broken friendships.

It is not something you were born with; it is the result of complex trauma that you went through when you were too young to process your emotions. While it is still diagnosed the same, BPD in women comes with its own set of unique challenges and experiences. The distinction is important because sometimes the first step in recovery from BPD is to have your particular struggles seen and your unique experiences validated.

The Stigma of BPD

Low self-esteem and self-image issues are among the core effects of BPD, which obviously contribute to the struggle. Besides having to deal with issues like these, people with BPD regularly carry shame surrounding their diagnosis, feeling as if they are too dramatic, too complicated, or broken beyond repair.

These feelings are often confirmed by the way other people treat them. From the outside, people see things like anger issues, impulsive and unpredictable behavior, and many damaged relationships, and cast blame. Being seen as the villain does not help someone who has a crippling fear of abandonment in every relationship they develop.

Besides this, people sometimes dismiss BPD as “attention-seeking behavior”, a bad attitude, or a toxic personality. BPD in women is a magnified issue because historically, women have been labeled as overly emotional, impulsive, or melodramatic.

The truth is that people with BPD were neglected at a vulnerable and critical phase of their development, with too many complex emotions and experiences to process. They are not too much; they simply had too much to deal with at too young an age.

Is BPD in women different?

While the diagnostic criteria for determining BPD do not change for women, and gender does not always affect the way BPD looks, certain critical aspects make BPD in women a unique experience. As with any mental health condition, the way it presents can look different depending on the individual, their age, their background, and a host of other things. It is the same condition, but it is sometimes displayed through different lenses.

At a certain age, emotional dysregulation becomes part of the monthly experience for many women. BPD in women generally means having to face more acute emotional instability, though. These are not the mood swings associated with hormones, either. With BPD, there are more intense emotions that shift rapidly and unpredictably and feel impossible to control.

All people with BPD experience bouts of emptiness and depression, but research shows that this is a more chronic issue for women with BPD. They tend to become suicidal more often than men and develop self-harming tendencies in most cases.

There are also unique combinations of disorders that women with BPD have to deal with that affect men less frequently. For example, it is common for BPD in women to exist alongside anxiety, eating disorders, and PTSD, while men more commonly tend to experience antisocial traits and substance abuse with BPD.

Without an official diagnosis for BPD, any one of the unique traits associated with the disorder could steal focus. A woman might believe she is depressed to the point of feeling suicidal, while also struggling in relationships and missing the fact that it is BPD causing each of these issues. One person’s experience with BPD might be different from someone else’s, even when they have a similar history and personality.

What BPD in Women Looks Like in Relationships

Relationships are the area that gives more clues to a person’s mental health struggles than anywhere else, particularly with BPD. Men and women tend to navigate friendships, romantic partnerships, and intimacy differently from each other, and with BPD, these differences can become a little more pronounced. On the other hand, BPD causes people to be unpredictable and emotionally unstable, regardless of their gender.

People with BPD will send intense mixed signals, from being almost obsessed with someone for a while before becoming disinterested in a short time. They might go from dismissing their partner’s needs and ignoring their preferences one day, to expressing their unfaltering devotion to the relationship the next.

These kinds of mood swings are often unfairly attributed to women in general, but these levels of unpredictable, toxic behavior often point to an underlying condition, whether in men or women.

For people with BPD, relationships and friendships will always be chaotic and complicated. They have the tendency to elevate certain people, romantic or otherwise, to a god-like status, before completely devaluing them without warning.

BPD brings with it more arguments, disagreements, and falling-outs than the average adult friend circle. When a person’s friendships and family connections are constantly fraught with drama and intensity, it should count as a warning sign pointing to a mental health struggle.

Statistically, fewer women are shown to have anger control issues with BPD than men. This does not mean that BPD in women does not cause anger or rage issues. People with BPD regularly respond with anger that is disproportionate to the situation.

Culturally, it might be more expected to see men in a towering rage over certain things because anger presents as a masculine emotion. Uncontrollable anger, however, often points to emotional regulation issues, especially when it doesn’t match the trigger.

Many people struggle with identity issues, confidence, and shifting goals; it’s part of growing up and finding your feet in life. People with BPD consistently struggle with their identity, and this affects everything, from their career goals to their relationships. They might be focused on a goal or a life plan for months, only to unexpectedly drop it and change directions.

From the outside, it looks like they are being inexplicably erratic, while inside, they are dealing with low self-confidence and fear of abandonment should they not meet their goal. A fear of being abandoned by others underpins almost every major decision in a person’s life when they are dealing with BPD.

BPD in women also regularly shows up in the impulsive way she handles her finances, in her constantly changing appearance, and in her hobbies and interests, particularly if they are constantly changing.

Each of these things will inevitably affect her relationships and close friendships, whether she is aware of it or not. Without knowing anything about BPD, she might be labeled as immature, impulsive, or toxic, when in truth she is dealing with something more difficult than others could ever realize.

Recovery From BPD in Women

Dealing with BPD is not a life sentence, and many people recover to the point that they no longer meet the criteria for diagnosis when retested. It is not an infectious disease that can be healed, but it is also not a condition someone is born with; it is a result of complex trauma that can be treated and resolved.

Women with BPD have to face struggles like stigma, stereotypes, misdiagnoses, gendered blame, and the systemic invalidation of their struggles, all as she deals with extreme emotions, low self-esteem, and a fear of abandonment. It could take years of employing evidence-based therapies, but it is possible to recover fully from BPD and have a life of unproblematic relationships and a secure attachment.

You are not alone as you deal with BPD. If you would like to research your options for therapy and support, we can help. We host an online catalog of counselors that we would love you to explore. We hope you find someone suitable to meet with. If you would rather speak with someone who can help you find a counselor, our reception team will be happy to help.

“Purple Flower”, Courtesy of Elodie Debard, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

item.title: When Do You Need a Christian Therapist?
item.description:
With recent events, more people are turning back to their Christian faith or discovering Jesus for the first time. Christian counseling is about helping people find ways to improve their mental health through a biblical perspective. Jesus broke His people free from the yokes and burdens of this life to live for Him, so we know we can break unhealthy and generational cycles through Him. A Christian therapist can get you on the right path toward healing.

Why People Choose a Christian Therapist

People inherently know there is more to life, even if they are unsure what it can be. We were made to worship something or someone. God created this innate desire to draw us closer to Him. Often, we get off track by the world and need help resetting our priorities. Yet, it is God who can heal us of every temptation and sin. We can lean on Him when we feel anxious, depressed, or out of control.

Topics Covered in Christian Therapy

Christian counseling covers a wide range of topics from family issues to severe mental health disorders. A Christian therapist specializes in specific areas and can bring their expertise to the session, combining evidence-based methods with faith-based principles. This combination helps people overcome problems while growing emotionally, mentally, and spiritually.

The following are several topics covered through Christian counseling.

Trauma

Trauma can occur after a sudden event or through long-term exposure. For example, a person may suffer the effects of trauma after a natural disaster or house fire. They can experience trauma after witnessing a crime or caring for a terminal loved one. The body’s response to trauma is to activate the fight-or-flight response, which can lead to anxiety disorders and depression.

Abandonment and Neglect

Abandonment and neglect during childhood can often lead to adult problems with self-esteem, confidence, and relationships. Children may withdraw or lash out as they try to find their place in this world and feel loved. This can lead to behavioral problems and depression.

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD with or without hyperactivity) can interfere with school, work, and relationships. Adults learn to cover up the symptoms of ADHD, but can still feel out of control and forgetful. Children with ADHD may feel misunderstood.

Anger Issues

Anger management is offered through a Christian therapist. Anger issues can stem from childhood, hormonal changes, or mental health disorders. Learning how to calm oneself and resolve conflict peacefully is a lifelong skill one can learn.

Anxiety

Anxious thoughts and worries can develop into anxiety disorders and Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD). The Bible tells us hundreds of times not to fear, and Jesus told us not to worry about tomorrow, yet our minds require constant renewing because we give in so easily to anxiety. Chemical imbalances in the brain can also contribute to high anxiety.

Depression

Depression can be dangerous if left untreated. Most people feel blue at least sometimes during their lifetime. However, depression can feel permanent and last for several weeks or months. It can lead to intrusive thoughts, self-harm, or suicide. Depression is often seen in teens and adults, although some children who have suffered trauma or abuse may develop depression.

Eating Disorders

Anorexia nervosa, bulimia, and binge eating are eating disorders that, if left untreated, can be fatal. In the case of anorexia, the body starves as nutrients are withheld. Eventually, this leads to organ failure. Bulimia, bingeing and purging food, can lead to physical conditions that endanger life. Binge eating can lead to problems, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol, heart attack, stroke, Type 2 diabetes, obesity, and a loss of self-worth.

Autism Spectrum Disorder

The autism spectrum is wide, and not everyone develops the same signs. Christian counseling can help children and adults move forward and not allow autism to be a barrier. People with autism can learn how to communicate, navigate social cues, and regulate emotions through therapy.

Bipolar Disorder

Bipolar disorder consists of manic episodes (highs) and depressive episodes (lows). This cycle can last weeks or months. In some cases, people with bipolar disorder may cycle quickly between manic and depressive states, which can confuse others at home, work, and in relationships.

Substance Abuse

Alcohol and drugs, including prescription drugs, can lead to addiction if abused. Substance abuse becomes a problem when you use it as a coping mechanism. These substances can lead to mental and physical issues, deteriorate relationships, and endanger your job.

Physical and Sexual Abuse

No one should ever experience physical, verbal, or sexual abuse. Yet, we live in a fallen world, and far too many people have suffered at the hands of others. Christian counseling is customized to your needs. Your Christian therapist will work with you to remove the power left behind by memories and words and replace them with the power of Jesus. You will learn strategies to overcome your past and move away from current toxic relationships.

Marriage or Relationship Problems

Every relationship or marriage has its issues. Learning to walk through them together can be hard. Christian counseling addresses premarital, relationship, and marriage problems. Areas that Christian therapists often work with clients on include premarital expectations, boundaries for in-laws, infidelity and affairs, financial strain, parenting disagreements, addiction, and grief.

Grief and Loss

Grief and loss can weigh one down. The grieving process is not linear. It consists of denial and shock, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. However, most people cycle through these stages several times, often staying in one stage longer than the others. When grief or loss interferes with your daily responsibilities and mental health over time, you may need a Christian therapist to help you cope and heal.

Family Issues

Family issues can vary from moving to a new city and schools to problems between parents or parents and children. Blended families may need family counseling to address the issues that can arise when two households become one. Family counseling is also helpful when one member of the family is struggling with a mental disorder, as the others learn how to support and encourage them.

Men’s and Women’s Issues

Counseling covers the areas that cause you the most concern, even the ones you might deem embarrassing. Christian counselors work with professionalism and want to help you overcome these issues. Counselors may work with men having erectile problems that interfere with their marriage, men and women struggling with the temptation of an emotional affair, or a woman admitting that she feels a distance from her children. Counseling is a safe space for these hard conversations.

Teen Problems

Teens have their own issues that impact their lives and families. Teen pregnancy, bullying, peer pressure, premarital sex, not feeling accepted, drug abuse, online predators, and targeted internet attacks can rob a child of their self-esteem and leave them confused. They can feel as if the weight of the world is on their shoulders. Teens who have experienced trauma or abuse may develop anxiety and depression. Teens are also at a higher risk of self-harm and suicide.

Spiritual Growth

Spiritual growth provides you with a foundation in the Word, knowledge about God, and a personal relationship with Jesus. It equips you to share the gospel with a hurt and fallen world. Spiritual growth helps you to rely on and trust that God has a bigger plan for your greater good. A Christian therapist will help you align your life to Scripture and follow Jesus, seeking God before making big decisions and turning your worries and hurts over to Him.

Finding a Christian Therapist in Your Area

If you are looking for a Christian therapist in your area, contact our team today. A representative will connect you with a Christian therapist. We offer virtual sessions to clients who may find it more relaxing to confide in the comfort of their own home. We also hold in-person and group counseling sessions. Call us today to learn more about how a Christian therapist and counseling can help you.

item.title: When Borderline Traits Go Unnoticed: The Hidden Patterns That Shape Daily Life
item.description:
We often think of mental health challenges as being a clear diagnosis with obvious symptoms. However, there are times when the signs are subtle. Borderline traits are one of those challenges that can exist beneath the surface, shaping relationships, emotions, and decision-making without ever being recognized for what they are.

Borderline traits are often dismissed as personality, quirks, or emotional sensitivity. The person experiencing them may feel like something is off, but they don’t know how to name it. These traits don’t always meet the threshold for a formal diagnosis, so they remain in the background, affecting daily life in ways that feel confusing and isolating.

Understanding these hidden patterns begins with asking what lies beneath them that feels familiar and frustrating. It’s a journey of curiosity and not judgment. In faith, you can come to God and ask for help:

Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! – Psalm 139:23, ESV

Borderline Traits and Emotional Intensity

The most common appearance of borderline traits is in the intensity of emotional responses. A minor disagreement can feel like a complete rupture, and a moment of perceived rejection can trigger overwhelming shame or anger. These involuntary reactions arise with a force that feels beyond control.

After experiencing these reactions, individuals often wonder why they responded so strongly. Friends and family often describe them as overly sensitive or dramatic, unaware that what they are witnessing is a nervous system that processes emotions at a heightened level.

The intensity goes beyond negative feelings. Joy can feel explosive, and excitement can quickly turn into anxiety. It is as if the individual experiences emotions without a dimmer switch, and everything is at full volume. The result is exhaustion for the person experiencing it and for those around them. This constant navigation of highs and lows becomes a way of life that feels normal even when it’s depleting.

Christian counselors recognize emotional intensity as a sign that the nervous system, from early on, learned to stay vigilant. The individual learns to read every signal as potentially dangerous. Healing from borderline traits and the intensity of emotions involves learning to regulate what feels uncontrollable and find safety in the presence of God and people you trust. God is faithful to help you in this place:

He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. – Psalm 147:3, ESV

Borderline Traits and the Fear of Abandonment in Relationships

Persistent fear that people will leave is one of the most painful aspects of undetected borderline traits. This is a deep dread that influences decisions, communications, and attachment. It is common for these individuals to repeatedly test relationships by pushing people away to see if they’ll come back.

Another response is to cling to people, fearing that any space will result in a permanent loss. Each response stems from the same core belief that they are fundamentally unworthy of staying.

It’s not a fear that is always present and clear. It could look like jealousy, control, or a constant need for reassurance. It may show up as an inability to be alone or, conversely, as a pattern of ending relationships before the other person has had a chance to leave first. It is a desperate attempt to avoid the pain of abandonment, even when the avoidance creates the very distance that they have feared.

Recognizing the fear is the first step toward addressing it. The process requires the individual to acknowledge how past experiences of loss or inconsistency have created a template for how their relationships feel. They have to learn to build new experiences that challenge the assumption that everyone will eventually leave.

The Unstable Sense of Self that Shifts with Circumstances

Those who struggle with undetected borderline traits often feel as if they do not know who they are. They also feel their sense of identity shift depending on who they are with, what role they play, or what feedback they receive. This is not an intentional deception. It is a genuine question about their own values, preferences, and personality.

Some individuals may adopt their romantic partner’s interests, only to change their minds when the relationship ends. These individuals often change career plans frequently in search of the right thing, but never quite find it.

The result of this unstable sense of self is a chronic feeling of emptiness. It is a sense of a core lacking that other people seem to have. This makes decision-making difficult because they lack an internal compass to provide guidance. These individuals often look to others for validation and try to piece together their identity from external feedback rather than from internal knowing.

Christian counselors help these individuals explore their identity in Christ. Together, they can lay a foundation that does not shift with circumstances and creates a stable reference point when everything else feels uncertain. This process involves separating what has been absorbed by the experiences from what is genuinely true for them.

The Impulsive Behaviors that Offer Temporary Relief

Impulsive behaviors offer a moment of relief when emotions feel unbearable, and the sense of self feels shaky. These behaviors may include spending money recklessly, engaging in risky sexual behavior, substance abuse, binge eating, or self-harm to name a few.

The function of the behavior is to provide a temporary escape from their experience of emotional pain or emptiness. It may feel that the behaviors are the only option at the time. Afterward, there is often shame and regret, which fuels more emotional pain and possibly more impulsive behavior.

These patterns are hard to address because they work temporarily. They become automatic responses to distress, which do provide relief but also reinforce impulsive behavior. The individuals who struggle with borderline traits may not even recognize the patterns of these behaviors until they are brought to their attention, or the consequences can no longer be ignored.

Breaking free from these impulsive patterns requires that an individual develop healthier ways to manage distress. This includes learning to tolerate uncomfortable emotions instead of immediately seeking escape. It is slow work that requires patience and support. It is encouraging to remember Scripture in this case:

No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it. – 1 Corinthians 10:13, ESV

Finding Clarity and Hope

Understanding and recognizing undetected borderline traits does not involve assigning a label. The goal is to find clarity for patterns that have felt confusing when someone cannot name what they have been experiencing. This will open the door to getting help and reduce the blame they place upon themselves for being too much or not enough. It gives them a pathway to address the underlying patterns with compassion and effective strategies.

This process involves therapy approaches such as dialectical behavior therapy to target emotional regulation, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness. Building a support system that can hold steady when emotions feel chaotic is another part of the process to address these traits. Deepening a relationship with God, who offers unconditional love, creates a foundation that does not shift with behavior or performance.

For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. – Romans 8:38-39, ESV

Taking the Next Step

Recognizing that you struggle with borderline trait patterns is a start toward better mental health. Reaching out for professional help is a crucial step, and it is not a weakness or failure. It’s important to find support that will encourage your journey toward healing through a faith-based process. Christian counselors are equipped to help you understand and identify borderline trait patterns and behavior.

Contact our reception team to learn more about your options and get started working with someone who can help you navigate emotional regulation and relationship patterns.

item.title: Emotional Burnout and the Hidden Guilt of Rest
item.description:
Not every kind of depletion announces itself right away; some just quietly settle in and stay. It builds up slowly in the early mornings and late nights. Lingering in the days that you pushed through, even though your body was screaming for rest.

When you decide to listen to your body, you find that instead of relief, you are faced with feelings of guilt, as if you are falling behind on something. It’s as if you have to earn rest before you are allowed to experience it. This is emotional burnout, and it makes rest feel like a problem rather than a remedy. This feeling has roots that run deeper than a full schedule or a season filled with demands.

In this, Jesus calls us to Himself:

“Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” – Matthew 11:28, NIV

The Mixed Signals Society Sends About Rest

Today’s culture suggests that rest is something you arrive at only after you have finished everything else. It is the mindset that says you rest once the work is done and the goals are met. It is a message that rings the bell of having to prove you deserve a break.

For those already depleted, this list never ends, which means rest never quite comes. The result is a balancing act where the body is trying to slow down, and the mind is running a constant argument of why stopping is not an option.

The outcome of this internal battle is a low-grade shame that follows anytime there is a moment of stillness. It is a persistent feeling that a person should be doing something more useful than breathing. And underneath all of this is a set of competing values between the belief that productivity equals worth and the belief that stopping means you are somehow less.

For many people, this belief did not begin in adulthood. It was shaped early on in households where rest was earned, where sitting still meant you were not contributing, and where being busy was treated as proof of being responsible. Over time, this conditioning deepens. As responsibilities increase with age, the pattern becomes so familiar that rest feels foreign, and any pause has to be justified before it can be accepted.

God tells us that rest and stillness are important:

He says, “Be still, and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth.” – Psalm 46:10, NIV

How Emotional Burnout Reshapes the Way You Experience Rest

When the nervous system operates under this prolonged pressure, urgency becomes the normal setting. This makes slowing down feel like a threat rather than a restorative action. Stillness becomes an unfamiliar territory for people experiencing high levels of chronic stress.

These individuals tend to have increased anxiety as they attempt to rest. Their system has adapted to a high state of alert, and when they step out of that, there is discomfort instead of peace. These individuals are unable to tolerate idleness, which is more common than most of us realize.

Christian counselors recognize that the inability to tolerate idleness is not failure or lack of discipline. It is a physiological and psychological response to the overwhelming busyness of carrying too much for too long. This response is going to require something more intentional than just a weekend away to unwind and refresh.

It calls for a deeper awareness of how the body has learned to associate stillness with danger and how the mind has been trained to equate doing nothing with falling behind. Without addressing this deeper pattern, even the most well-intended attempts at rest will feel incomplete or unsettling rather than restorative.

God’s heart for us is renewal and restoration:

…but those who hope in the LORD will renew their strength. They will soar on wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not be faint. – Isaiah 40:31, NIV

The Spiritual Layer of Emotional Burnout

Believers face a challenge with rest that carries a spiritual weight often overlooked. Faith communities celebrate dedication, service, and sacrifice. These values can generate competing demands and make it difficult to separate devotion from depletion. This could lead to a distorted understanding of what faithfulness actually asks.

God does not speak of rest as self-indulgence or a lack of trust. Doing less is not an indication of spiritual irresponsibility. These things are part of being a good steward of the body that God has given us.

When emotional burnout goes unaddressed within this context of faith, there is an added layer of weight in feeling as though they have let God down. Christian counselors emphasize that for those who serve in ministry, caregiving, or other high-demand callings, rest is not an absence of faithfulness. They encourage the understanding that rest is a rhythm that God established in the beginning of creation.

Then, because so many people were coming and going that they did not even have a chance to eat, he said to them, “Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest.” – Mark 6:31, NIV

What It Looks Like to Rest Toward Healing

After a prolonged period of depletion, reclaiming rest is not about doing less. To fully rest after this type of weariness requires the individual to unlearn the beliefs that made rest feel unsafe. It is a willingness to examine the idea of value being tied to output or that productivity is proof of faithfulness. Rest in its most genuine form goes beyond sleep and includes emotional safety, relational connection, physical recovery, and spiritual nourishment.

This may look like learning to sit in stillness without immediately reaching for a task. It may involve allowing yourself to say no without feeling the need to explain. It is recognizing that fatigue is not laziness, but the body communicating a real and valid need that has gone unmet for too long. Reclaiming rest means permitting yourself to be present in your own life without the pressure of producing something in return.

Christian counselors are trained to help individuals identify which layers of rest have been missing and how to build rhythms that are sustainable and rooted in theology and grounded in the body and soul. This journey to genuine wholeness does not happen in a single decisive moment. It requires deliberate choices to stop, receive, and trust God in an act of deep faith toward long-lasting healing.

There remains, then, a Sabbath-rest for the people of God; for anyone who enters God’s rest also rests from their own works, just as God did from his. – Hebrews 4:9-10, NIV

Finding Freedom From Emotional Burnout

If rest feels wrong, you’re not alone. It’s not a sign of weakness or evidence of spiritual failure, but rather it is a result of carrying more than you should for longer than your body can sustain. The goal of rest after being depleted for so long is not to feel shame. It is to understand why stopping feels difficult and to find a path back to the rest that restores, instead of merely pausing.

God did not design us to run ourselves into the ground, even in the service of doing good. We were designed to rest after work. It is not a reward for doing something good. Choosing to understand the goodness of rest in God’s plan is a courageous step that leads to long-lasting wholeness.

If you or a loved one is navigating emotional exhaustion and finds it difficult to slow down, reach out to our reception team. They can connect you with the right person to help you navigate the balance between rest and getting everything done.

item.title: Christian-Based Counseling in Texas: Keys to Success
item.description:
Everyone strives for success, at least in one area of their lives or another, and Christian-based counseling in Texas can help. Some might consider success to be measured by the numbers in their bank account, and some might say that they’ll be a success when they hit a certain number of friends or followers on social media.

Others strive for prestige or social status in their community, aspiring to be a member of a certain social circle or club. Christians or religious people might define success differently, saying true success comes from laying down your life for others or following a preset career path in ministry.

No matter how you define success, chances are great that you’re striving for it. You may even be frustrated at the elusive nature of your goals. Success, even if it seems out of your grasp, is achievable if you embrace a few key concepts. While circumstances and opportunities vary, these principles consistently increase the likelihood of meaningful success.

Curiosity Leads to Success

Curiosity is not always celebrated in our culture. Think of all the mischief Curious George got into just because of his curiosity. The curious neighbor is often portrayed as the local gossip in popular media, and kids are sometimes told not to ask so many questions when parents don’t want to talk about a subject.

While this seems to be the cultural narrative, viewing curiosity in a negative way is damaging. Curiosity is what leads to knowledge, new experiences, and eventually, success.

Children are naturally curious. They love to explore new places and try new things. Unfortunately, adulthood has a way of stymying that curiosity in most people. But when you allow yourself to stay curious into adulthood, you permit yourself to learn. That mindset shift can change everything in your life. Curious people ask better questions, notice opportunities that others might overlook, and are far more willing to try new things, even if it means risking failure.

Curiosity pushes you to grow and explore because your desire to understand is so overwhelming that it compels you to learn. This mindset turns you from being a stymied passive bystander into an active, engaged participant in your own life.

Humility Leads to Success

Humility is another important element on the road to success. Humility is often associated with relational success, but it also plays a part in being successful in other areas of your life as well. How does being humble affect your success in business, ministry, and education, outside of its relational value?

Being humble leads to asking questions. Curiosity creates the desire to learn, but humility is what allows you to admit that you still need to. If you already think you know it all, you’re not as likely to succumb to your own curiosity. You won’t ask questions or try to learn from others because your pride tells you that you don’t need to.

If you’re full of pride, you’re also less likely to take constructive criticism. Everyone, even those with mounds of experience and skill, can make mistakes. When these inevitable mistakes happen, you can either acknowledge them and accept the occasional correction or you can blame others or circumstances. When you don’t own up to your mistakes, you miss an opportunity to grow. Not only is it a part of the growth process, but humility is a vital part of the formula for success.

Discipline Leads to Success

Being curious and humble is necessary, but if you aren’t able to sustain them, they’ll do you little good. Discipline, or perhaps another way of thinking of it, consistency, is also a key element to success.

Being disciplined requires you to learn how to live in the uncomfortable. In a society that values comfort with pillow-top beds and instant microwavable meals, it can be off-putting to live without comforts. But if you want to succeed in life, you have to learn how to survive and eventually thrive when you would rather leave or change your situation.

When you consistently put one foot in front of the other, systematically going through the steps that will lead to success, you will eventually see progress. The unfortunate reality is that many people with great ability and skill falter because they’re not disciplined enough to stay the course when the path becomes uncomfortable.

Biblical Advice

The Bible, the ultimate authority for guiding believers, agrees with the value of curiosity, humility, and discipline.

Scripture implores you to seek understanding and wisdom. In other words, the Bible tells you to be curious. Proverbs 25 says, “It is the glory of God to conceal a matter; to search out a matter is the glory of kings.” (Proverbs 25:2, NIV)

This verse eloquently discusses the profound tension that exists between the mystery of the universe and the human drive to understand it. There are aspects of existence and complexities of the universe that provide you with the why behind your curiosity.

God’s glory to conceal acknowledges that these truths remain intentionally complex or hidden. But conversely, the glory of kings is where you come in. The glory lies in the diligent labor of investigating your world. This Scripture suggests that one of the highest human achievements is to peel back those unknown layers of obscurity through research and analysis.

This curiosity and pursuit of knowledge are honorable to God and are God-given traits. He doesn’t flinch at our questions or discourage us from knowledge. He invites us to seek Him instead, and this is the source of real wisdom.

Humility, too, is championed and provides a central theme throughout the Bible. James 4:10 reminds us that if you humble yourself before the Lord, He will lift you up. True success in God’s eyes isn’t found in pride or in self-promotion. It’s the recognition that you’re dependent on Him and that you’re willing to learn from others.

In 1 Corinthians 9:24-27, Paul compares the Christian life to a race that requires training and perseverance. In other words, discipline. Success, like the Christian life, isn’t achieved overnight but requires consistency and a willingness to stay committed even when it’s difficult and even when it’s uncomfortable.

Different Goals, Same Principles

While the principles of curiosity, humility, and discipline are universal, the success they produce can look different depending on your focus. Worldly success is often centered on the accumulation of wealth, status, or influence. It’s a destination-based success.

Biblical success is measured in the transformation of your heart and defines who you are. It looks even more closely at who you are becoming and who you belong to. It’s valued in stewardship. It is not in what you have but how you’re using what you’ve already been given.

Despite these different finish lines, the mechanics of the race remain identical. The same curiosity a CEO uses to innovate a project is the curiosity a believer uses to study the depths of Scripture. The same discipline an athlete uses to train for a marathon is the discipline a person uses to maintain a consistent prayer life or to break an ingrained habit.

God has given us a powerful toolkit that helps us live successfully both in our relationship with him and the world around us.

Christian-Based Counseling in Texas: Therapy Supports Success

True success is the integration of your outward actions with your internal dialogue. It’s the realization that “searching out a matter” includes searching out the why behind your anxiety or understanding why you can’t seem to overcome a certain behavior.

Therapy can be a useful tool to help you achieve success, both in worldly and spiritual terms. When you peel back the layers of your own life, you are using your curiosity to drive success. In therapy, you will learn how to develop a sense of curiosity and humility and how to be consistent, even when uncomfortable.

Call our office to discuss how Christian-based counseling in Texas can help you find your own keys to success.

item.title: How Social Media Algorithms Can Affect Self-Esteem
item.description:
In the modern age of technology, social media platforms have become not only a means of communication/connection but a way of seeking psychological comfort. Various social media platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, Meta, and YouTube use algorithms to assess your perceived interests and continue showing feeds of those interests.

But what exactly is an algorithm, and can it change? What is the connection between these algorithms and one’s interpretation of self-esteem? Who is mostly impacted by this occurrence? This article will focus on these primary questions, outcomes, and alternatives to address a growing concern of social media use among America’s youth.

Algorithms

Per the Merriam-Webster dictionary, an algorithm is “a step-by-step set of instructions or rules used to solve a problem, perform a calculation, or complete a specific task.” Simply put, different platforms, including social media, use algorithms to target content that is perceived to be preferred by the person using various feeds on social media.

The algorithms on social media are set by the duration of a video watched. For example, if a person scrolls past several videos but watches a video for thirty seconds or more, an algorithm is created to show you more videos of similar content.

For instance, if you enjoy watching videos of people doing do-it-yourself (DIY) projects and watch various DIY videos, the algorithm will show you predominantly DIY videos. These algorithms are typically broken when a new algorithm is created based on a perceived change of interest, or you spend more time on different feeds. On most social media platforms, you can have more than one algorithm depending on your interests.

Connection of Algorithms and Self-Esteem

Now that we know what an algorithm is and how it works, what impact does it have on one’s self-esteem? Think of a particular feed that may touch an insecurity of yours. For example, maybe you are having a rather difficult time in life, and you see more videos of people demonstrating happiness, wealth, etc., and now these videos cause a psychological reaction.

This can be as simple as “I was already having a horrible day because of work, now I see other people happy at their jobs on TikTok, and I feel worse now about my situation.” For many adults, compared to adolescents/teenagers, social media may serve as a temporary or even regular outlet to disconnect from day-to-day stressors.

However, these algorithms pose a risk of developing a sense of dependence on them to relieve stress, anxiety, or bring happiness (e.g., laughter from videos you find hilarious). Therefore, there are potentially consequential implications of this depending on the algorithms you have and the frequency of your social media use.

Who is impacted or how is someone affected?

Social media has different impacts on different age groups. First, let’s look at the social and psychological impacts on American youth. One of the largest concerns is the prevalence of cyberbullying, and leading to riskier behaviors among youth.

According to Khalaf, et. al. (2023), American youth who are overly exposed to social media, particularly in late adolescence and teenage years, are at higher risk of developing psychopathology such as clinical depression, anxiety and/or phobia disorders, and suicidal ideation.

Per their study, researchers found that 14.8% of adolescent psychiatric admissions to hospitals between 2016 and 2020 reported that the primary reason for their admission was due to cyberbullying on social media, which led to them feeling overwhelming suicidal ideation (Khalaf, et. al., 2023).

This research study also found a significant correlation between before and/or during bedtime use of social media/technology and poorer sleep and eventual academic decline. Additional concerns consist of unmonitored activities on social media platforms that depict pseudo pornographic content.

This has resulted in a high prevalence among adolescents and teenagers using pornography, which can cause several other psychological and physiological challenges. Positive uses of social media include better awareness of the importance of taking care of one’s mental health, humor content, identity formation, and creative expression.

Now let’s compare this to adults. Similar to youth, social media serves as a multi-purposed outlet for everyday life. However, the risks are different and often more damaging compared to youth. For instance, employers in the last ten years have used social media posts of their employees as justifications for terminating their employment.

In addition, with vast amounts of knowledge on social media, threats of violence have exponentially increased, including threats to find where people live, work, or where their children go to school. According to Naslund, et. al. (2020), an estimated 3.8 billion people in the world had access to social media in 2020, which included a large demographic of adults living with mental illnesses.

This exposed adults with and without serious mental illnesses to influences that challenge or question one’s reality. For example, with the various conspiracy theories circulating on social media, adults who live with conditions like schizophrenia are more prone to having their existing symptoms become more severe (Naslund, et. al., 2020).

Additionally, social media use has significantly impacted in-person social interactions. Following the COVID-19 pandemic, many adults found that a temporary method of communication (i.e., due to government isolation regulations) never reverted to previous methods of communication.

This includes fewer social interactions and difficulty handling social conflicts in an appropriate manner. This became even more prevalent when social media trends such as recording altercations became popular as a form of entertainment and with a disregard for law, order, or civility. In fact, these social media trends have gained such popularity that certain platforms pay you to watch them, which triggers more algorithms.

What is the impact of social media on Christianity?

Social media has had a two-fold impact on Christianity. On one side, Christianity continues to be vilified as a hateful religion that ostracizes anyone who does not think, feel, or believe in every word of the Bible. For example, while at a Mariners game at T-Mobile Park in Seattle, you might see a group of people with signs saying that a certain demographic of people (often an explicit or vulgar adjective) “…are going to hell, repent now or be judged!”

This video and several others like it flood social media platforms and convince several people (youth and adults alike) that Christianity is a hateful religion. This is largely seen in major U.S. metropolitan cities across the country in universities, colleges, high schools, and public events. This not only makes it difficult to convince others of the good news of Jesus Christ, but it tarnishes its validity in their eyes.

The other side is a great promotion of Christianity. Specifically, having younger adults worshiping God influences other youth and even adults to give their lives over to God. Social media platforms in the last five years have even been used by churches across the United States to promote community events and overall advertisement of the church. However, depending on the algorithm, people can be influenced either positively or negatively.

What is a potential solution to harmful social media use?

Simple options include limiting social media use as an adult and really understanding your daily dependence on it. If you feel you cannot get off social media despite overt negative repercussions, seek professional help, as you may be demonstrating addictive-type behaviors.

Limit screen time for youth and have appropriate parental locks as needed. Parents should have regular conversations with their kids about social media use and make sure they are doing okay. Practice having more conversations in person and do not recklessly debate people on social media (especially people you do not know).

References:
Khalaf, A. M., Alubied, A. A., Khalaf, A. M., & Rifaey, A. A. (2023). The impact of social media on the mental health of adolescents and young adults: A Systematic Review. Cureus, 15(8), e42990. href=”https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.42990″>https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.42990
Naslund, J. A., Bondre, A., Torous, J., & Aschbrenner, K. A. (2020). Social media and mental health: Benefits, risks, and opportunities for research and practice. Journal of technology in Behavioral Science, 5(3), 245–257. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41347-020-00134-x

Photos:
“Phone Users”, Courtesy of Camilo Jimenez, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; “Social Media”, Courtesy of dole777, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; “Texting”, Courtesy of Robin Worrall, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; “Social Media”, Courtesy of Julian, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post How Social Media Algorithms Can Affect Self-Esteem appeared first on Tacoma Christian Counseling.

item.title: From Taboo to Therapy: The Journey of Gen X Mental Health Wellness
item.description:
Generation X represents people born between 1965 and 1980. It is a quiet generation between the idealism of baby boomers and the outspoken awareness of millennials. This is where the term “The Forgotten Generation” stems from. In the Gen X world, independence was prized, and emotional toughness was highly valued.

There were only whispered conversations about mental health, and often, the subject was dismissed entirely. For many individuals in Gen X, survival meant being silent about their emotional pain. Mental health wellness for Gen X is now transforming a generation that was once overlooked into one that recognizes and values mental well-being.

As this generation navigates midlife, they balance careers, families, aging parents, and their faith. And in the midst of this, they have discovered that the inner silence of their youth has come with consequences.

Many Gen X adults wrestle with anxiety, loneliness, or emotional exhaustion underneath their competence and calmness. “Keep it together” was the cultural message of their youth. But faith reminds them that God never intended for people to carry the weight of their hearts alone.

…For the Lord sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart. – 1 Samuel 16:7, ESV

Growing Up Under the Weight of Mental Health Taboo

The Gen X story is often portrayed in terms of resilience. This generation is when latchkey kids became a household role. These kids came home to empty houses, heating leftovers in microwaves, and learning independence early. However, what was once labeled as self-reliance was sometimes masked as emotional neglect. Many in this generation were taught that strength meant silence.

Even in many church settings, culturally, the expressions of emotions were met with caution. Tears were for the weak, depression was something to pray about privately, and for those of faith, counseling was considered unnecessary.

Gen X learned to compartmentalize, separating emotions from spirituality and faith from vulnerability. The mental health and wellness of Gen X individuals focused on how well they could maintain their strength regardless of what was going on within themselves.

During this time, the church focused on behavior and doctrine, but hardly ever on emotional health. From the pulpit, Gen X was taught holiness in obedience. Trauma, anxiety, or need for emotional restoration was seldom addressed. Many Gen X believers grew to love God deeply, yet they struggled to believe that He cared about their inner pain.

Faith asks that we be honest about sin as well as sorrow. God delights in the truth regarding all of our being, even in the deepest places of our minds. This is an invitation that challenges the old taboo of silence and opens the door for authentic spiritual wellness for Gen X individuals.

The Hidden Struggles of Gen X

The individuals of Gen X have achieved a great deal when viewed from the outside. They are dependable, competent, and quite effective. But beneath that steadiness lies a generation that has carried more emotional weight than they were taught to manage.

This has resulted in many individuals living with the effects of chronic stress and suppressed emotions. Some battle depression or anxiety, and they hesitate to seek help because they have been taught they should handle it. Others carry unhealed childhood wounds, such as neglect, divorce, or instability.

In midlife, the unspoken burdens often surface, creating a need for relief from burdens they were never meant to carry. Balancing teenage children and aging parents creates emotional strain. Coupled with careers that once felt purposeful and friendships that are harder to maintain, GenX often experience a crisis of faith and wonder if God still sees them amid the demands of everyone else’s needs.

Christian counselors emphasize that Scripture reminds believers that God not only sees, but He also sustains. This doesn’t mean that emotions should be suppressed instead. It is an invitation to release it. They remind Gen X individuals that God understands emotions, and they don’t need to keep carrying weight that was never meant to be carried alone.

Cast your burden on the Lord, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved. – Psalm 55:22, ESV

Faith and Feelings: A Revisited Tension

Many Gen X Christians feel as though emotional honesty is risky. During their youth, the church culture often defined faith as the solution to every struggle and left little room for lament or any open conversation regarding mental health. When faced with an overwhelming situation, they were often told to pray about it. This resulted in the ability to hide emotions, keep struggles a secret, and remain strong on the outside.

Prayer is powerful, but without acknowledgment of pain, it becomes another form of denial. Jesus modeled emotional transparency. He wept over Lazarus’s death. He grieved over Jerusalem and anguished in Gethsemane. Jesus did not hide his feelings. Still, a generation of emotional suppression can’t be dismantled when they read that Jesus wept.

These words affirm that tears are not an indicator of a lack of faith, but rather an expression of its fullness. These examples validate any emotional expression as part of spiritual life. For Gen X believers, this truth means rediscovering the heart of faith that integrates mind, soul, and emotion under God’s care.

From Stigma to Seeking Help: Mental Health Wellness for Gen X

Slowly, this generation is moving forward to seek help without shame. What was once seen as a weakness is now recognized as a tool for healing. Gen X is no longer afraid of mental health wellness. The change is not about abandoning faith. It’s about transforming and aligning faith with truth.

Therapy, combined with prayer, brings things to the surface. Through the guidance of wise counselors, pastors, and mental health professionals, Gen X individuals come to understand God’s extension of grace.

Counseling is a biblical tool that God can use to bring restoration. Faith and therapy can work together to promote healing that affects both the mind and the soul. Through listening, empathy, and understanding, Christian counselors provide a pathway for Gen X Christians to experience a spiritual awakening that overcomes the stigma of being a latchkey kid. Gen X is learning that vulnerability does not weaken faith, and the courage to seek help is not a rejection of prayer.

The Role of the Church Today

Today’s church has an opportunity to redeem what was once neglected. Many Gen X believers are serving in leadership, raising children, mentoring the younger generation, or guiding ministries. They are becoming more emotionally honest in the church. Those who feel unseen can find a refuge in churches that address mental health with compassion and biblical truth.

Pastors and ministry leaders who encourage counseling and openness help dismantle the old taboo that faith and therapy are mutually exclusive. Encouragement and support are spiritual disciplines that create space for confession, lament, and healing. The churches that promote this reflect the heart of Christ, who forgives and restores.

Hope and Restoration for a Healing Generation

Gen X may have learned how to be silent in their childhood, but many are now discovering a new language of grace. They are learning to rest, admit their weaknesses, and believe that God’s strength is made perfect in their imperfections.

Even though they face fatigue or reflection in their midlife, some are beginning to see it as a season of renewal. They now understand that the God who saw their quiet endurance as children is now inviting them to experience His rest as adults.

And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. – 1 Peter 5:10, ESV

Wellness Is Possible

Standing at a crossroads, carrying the memory of what was and the promise of transformation, Gen X individuals are now able to grasp the openness of healing in the form of faith-based Christian counseling. They are learning how to dismantle the walls that helped them survive so they can be restored.

Connecting with a Christian counselor can lead to a transformed life that is not based on hiding emotions. By learning to implement skills that break the walls of silence and heal childhood wounds, Gen X individuals can experience mental health wellness that encourages them to find strength amid restoration.

For more information about overcoming the taboo mindset about mental health wellness, contact your local Christian counseling service. Begin your journey to breaking free from the silence of living strong as a Gen X individual.

item.title: Anxiety Disorders: What They Are and What to Do
item.description:
What is anxiety?

We’ve all felt anxious about something. Adrenaline rushes in. Cortisol gives us that unmistakable sense of dread. Our heart races. Breathing becomes shallow. We tense up and sweat buckets, our head pounds, and our stomach aches.

While not a pleasant experience, anxiety can be a normal human response to stressors in our environment. Normal anxiety is a temporary and realistic response to pressures such as taking a test or interviewing for a job. Once the event is over, the anxiety resolves.

Anxiety is a God-given reaction meant to protect us from dangerous situations. When we feel unsafe, our body responds with one of four mechanisms: fight, flight, freeze, and fawn. Most of us are familiar with the first three. The fourth is a learned trauma response “where a person finds themselves responding to someone they perceive as dangerous by engaging in people-pleasing and submissive behaviors” (Fawning Trauma Response: Why It Happens & How to Stop, 2024).

These four responses in themselves do not signal that a person has an anxiety disorder. They are usually brief, resolve in minutes, and are triggered in proportionate response to our environment. So, when exactly does anxiety meet the criteria?

Diagnostic Manual Definition of Anxiety Disorders

Anxiety disorders, according to the DSM-5-TR, the American Psychiatric Association’s diagnostic manual, are “disorders that share features of excessive fear and anxiety… Anxiety disorders differ from developmentally normative fear or anxiety by being excessive or persisting beyond developmentally appropriate periods…typically lasting 6 months or more” (American Psychiatric Association, 2022).

Consequently, the level and duration of fear and anxiety are key factors in what comprises a disorder. For example, two weeks spent stressing over an interview is normal. Suffering months of debilitating dread about the idea of being interviewed, and then sabotaging future employment opportunities because of it, is not.

Jesus tells us in Matt. 6:34 to avoid spending our life in chronic anxiety. He instructs us instead to deal with each day’s troubles as they come and not worry about troubles that haven’t yet taken place. He wasn’t just giving us a set of rules. Jesus knew that chronic worry leads to great harm if left unchecked.

Harmful Impacts of Chronic Anxiety

Healthline online breaks down the different impacts that long-term exposure to high stress has on the body. Physically, it can lead to excessive weight gain or loss. Cardiovascular issues could also arise, such as high blood pressure and heart disease, which increase the risk of coronary events such as heart attacks.

Other problems include digestive issues such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) or chronic infections. Those with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) “may be at an increased risk of hospitalization from anxiety-related complications” (Cherney, 2022). Muscle tension, depression, and isolation from social activities compound the issue.

Neurologically, the impacts of chronic stress are just as damaging. Stress triggers the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. This is the primary pathway that kicks in the fight, flight, freeze, and fawn reflexes. When the HPA is activated for too long, this can cause:

  • Hormonal imbalances that affect mood and cognition
  • Neurochemical disruptions that interfere with serotonin and dopamine (key players in emotional regulation)
  • Overstimulation of the amygdala, making you more anxious or reactive
  • Damage to the hippocampus, which is vital for memory and learning
  • Reduced function in the prefrontal cortex, impairing focus, planning, and decision-making (The Connection Between Stress and Neurological Disorders, 2025).

When fight, flight, freeze, and fawn remain in overdrive, the autonomic nervous system never allows for the “parasympathetic (“rest and digest”) system that helps you recover” (Ibid). The brain needs this permission to rest and digest. Without it, lasting changes occur in the structure and function of the brain, which can lead to depression and/or anxiety disorders from an overstimulated amygdala (Ibid).

Types of Anxiety Disorders

Now that we have an idea of how anxiety affects the body and brain, let’s take a closer look at the actual disorders and their diagnostic criteria. Please note that this is a general overview of each disorder. It is not meant to be used for personal diagnosis. If you believe you or someone you know might have an anxiety disorder, please reach out to a licensed mental health professional for help.

The following are general overviews from the DSM-5-TR:

Generalized Anxiety Disorder: Diagnostic Criteria

Includes excessive anxiety about events or activities (such as work or school performance). Signs and symptoms are:

  • Restlessness
  • Getting tired easily
  • Difficulty concentrating or mind going blank
  • Irritability
  • Muscle tension
  • Poor sleep

Panic Disorder

Includes recurrent unexpected panic attacks. Symptoms of a panic attack include:

  • Palpitations, pounding heart, or accelerated heart rate
  • Sweating
  • Trembling or shaking
  • Sensations of shortness of breath or smothering
  • Feelings of choking
  • Chest pain or discomfort
  • Nausea or abdominal distress
  • Feeling dizzy, unsteady, light-headed, or faint
  • Chills or heat sensations
  • Paresthesia (numbness or tingling sensations)
  • Derealization (feelings of unreality) or depersonalization (being detached from oneself)
  • Fear of losing control or “going crazy”
  • Fear of dying

Agoraphobia

Includes excessive anxiety about two (or more) of the following five situations:

  • Using public transportation
  • Being in open spaces
  • Being in enclosed places
  • Standing in line or being in a crowd
  • Being outside of the home alone

Social Anxiety Disorder

Includes excessive anxiety about social situations. (Some examples: having a conversation, meeting a stranger, being observed eating or drinking, performing in front of others – e.g., giving a speech). The person fears negative evaluation, such as being humiliated or embarrassed, and being rejected by or offending others.

Specific Phobias

Includes excessive anxiety about a specific object or situation (e.g., flying, heights, animals, receiving an injection, seeing blood). The phobic object or situation provokes anxiety that is out of proportion to the actual danger posed by the specific object or situation.

Separation Anxiety in Adults

Includes developmentally inappropriate and excessive anxiety concerning separation from attachment figures. The individual may show:

  • Excessive distress about being separated from home or from major attachment figures.
  • Excessive worry about losing major attachment figures or about possible harm to them, such as illness, injury, disasters, or death.
  • Excessive worry about experiencing an untoward event (e.g., getting lost, being kidnapped, having an accident, becoming ill) that causes separation from a major attachment figure.
  • Reluctance or refusal to go out, away from home, to school, to work, or elsewhere because of fear of separation.
  • Excessive fear of or reluctance about being alone or without major attachment figures at home or in other settings.
  • Reluctance or refusal to sleep away from home or to go to sleep without being near a major attachment figure.
  • Repeated nightmares involving the theme of separation.
  • Repeated complaints of physical symptoms when separation from major attachment figures occurs or is anticipated.

The fear, anxiety, or avoidance is persistent, lasting at least 4 weeks in children and adolescents and typically 6 months or more in adults (Ibid).

OCD and PTSD

While OCD and PTSD are not classified as anxiety disorders, they do share overlapping mechanisms, including excessive fear or anxiety that significantly impact vocational and social functioning. It’s important to get help with these or any of the other disorders on the list, as they significantly affect daily functioning.

How Anxiety Manifests in Daily Life

Anxiety disorders negatively influence relational, educational, or vocational functioning. While acute stress might cause occasional disruption such as missing a day of work, chronic stress from an anxiety disorder has a much more outsized impact. Some of these impacts include:

Workplace – Procrastination, over-preparation, avoidance of meetings, burnout, loss of employment.

Relationships – Reassurance seeking, people-pleasing behaviors, conflict avoidance, explosive confrontations, emotional withdrawal.

Parenting – Hypervigilance, overprotection, difficulty tolerating child distress, or dissociation.

Decision-making – Rumination, fear of mistakes, avoidance behaviors, sticking with what is safe.

Treatments

These impacts can seem overwhelming. It may seem as if nothing can be done to resolve the never-ending cycle of dread that comes with having an anxiety disorder. But the following therapies from qualified mental health professionals are effective treatments:

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): A licensed therapist trained in CBT helps clients identify, understand, and modify their anxiety-related thought and behavior patterns through regular sessions.

Dialectical Behavioral Therapy (DBT): DBT incorporates the philosophical practice of dialectics, in which multiple or even contradictory ideas are examined, combining acceptance and change at the same time.

Exposure therapy: A form of therapy involving gradually exposing the individual to feared situations in a safe and controlled environment, with the ultimate aim of reducing the associated anxiety.

Group therapy: Refers to therapeutic settings that involve multiple participants in addition to a single healthcare provider (Anxiety.org, 2016).

Somatic Therapies: Somatically based therapies such as EMDR, IFS, or Lifespan Integration help individuals to integrate sources of trauma that may have triggered the initial disorder.

SSRIs, SNRIs, and Other Medications: While not therapies, antidepressants have been proven to be effective treatments.

Techniques for Managing Anxiety:

It’s good to note that we can also improve our anxiety prognosis through managing our own behaviors, emotions, and thoughts. This can be seen with techniques such as:

  • Mindfulness exercises and deep breathing exercises, prayer, or meditation.
  • Physical activities such as running, walking, yoga, cycling, etc.
  • Practicing good nutrition and limiting sugar, alcohol, and caffeine (The Connection Between Stress and Neurological Disorders, 2025).

Conclusion

Anxiety disorders are common and impact millions of people every day. With proper diagnosis, therapy, and techniques, anxiety can be treated. God desires our wholeness. As the Bible says:

…for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control. – 2 Timothy 1:7 ESV

References:
American Psychiatric Association. (2022). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th-TR). American Psychiatric Association. https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.books.9780890425787
Anxiety.org. (2016, December 9). Anxiety.org. Anxiety.Org. https://www.anxiety.org/treatments
Cherney, K. (2022, September 19). Effects of Anxiety on the Body. Healthline. https://www.healthline.com/health/anxiety/effects-on-body#excretory-and-digestive
Fawning Trauma Response: Why It Happens & How to Stop. (2024). ChoosingTherapy.Com. https://www.choosingtherapy.com/fawning/
The Connection Between Stress and Neurological Disorders. (2025). Michiganneurologyassociates.Com.  https://www.michiganneurologyassociates.com/blog/the-connection-between-stress-and-neurological-disorders

Photos:
“Pumpkin”, Courtesy of Nikhita Singhal, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; “Pumpkin”, Courtesy of Aaron Burden, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post Anxiety Disorders: What They Are and What to Do appeared first on Seattle Christian Counseling.
